Unit arithmetic gives a dimension too: `1.watt * 1.hour` is a `Measure<Quantity.Energy>`, from the products `Units.SI` declares, and a product it does not declare is a type error.

entries.name: Area
entries.summary: Dimensions derived from others by the products and quotients in `Units.SI`: length over time is speed, speed over time acceleration, force over length pressure, and length squared area.

entries.name: Measure
entries.summary:
A quantity with a unit, of dimension `D`, one of the `Quantity` types.

Every unit module uses this record. `canonical` holds the value in the dimension's base unit and `unit` decides how it is shown, which is how +1.hour + 30.minute+ comes out right and still prints in hours.

entries.name: Duration
entries.summary:
A span of time, which is any measure of time.

`Time`, `Date` and `DateTime` take one: +Date.today() + 3.day+.

entries.name: TimeUnit
entries.summary: The units of time, from nanoseconds to weeks. The base unit is the second.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
Time measures from an `Integer`: `5.second`, `90.minute`, `2.week`.

The measure is shown in the unit you named, so `90.minute` prints as minutes, though it holds 5400 seconds as its base value.

entries.name: nanosecond
entries.summary: This many nanoseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: microsecond
entries.summary: This many microseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: millisecond
entries.summary: This many milliseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns this many seconds, as a `Measure`. The second is the base unit of time.

entries.name: minute
entries.summary: This many minutes, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: hour
entries.summary: This many hours, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: day
entries.summary: This many days, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: week
entries.summary: This many weeks, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary: Time measures from a `Float`, for fractional amounts: `1.5.hour`, `0.25.second`.

entries.name: nanosecond
entries.summary: This many nanoseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: microsecond
entries.summary: This many microseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: millisecond
entries.summary: This many milliseconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: This many seconds, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: minute
entries.summary: This many minutes, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: hour
entries.summary: This many hours, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: day
entries.summary: This many days, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: week
entries.summary: This many weeks, as a `Measure`.

entries.name: Measure<D>
signatures: to(String: Type, in: TimeUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary:
Equality and ordering of measures by quantity: `1.minute == 60.second` and `1.kilometer == 1000.meter`, whatever units each was written in.

Measures of different dimensions are never equal, and ordering them, as in `1.second < 1.meter`, is a type error. A measure whose dimension is only known at run time, made by unit arithmetic, is compared by its base-unit value alone.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(String: Type, in: TimeUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary: Renders the measure in its own unit.

entries.name: scaled
entries.summary:
Returns the measure in the largest unit in which its size is at least 1.

Time picks from nanoseconds through weeks, data from bytes through terabytes, and SI dimensions from the decimal prefixes nano through giga. Zero is shown in the base unit, and a value smaller than the smallest unit in that unit. Measures of other dimensions keep their unit.

entries.name: scaled
entries.summary: Returns the measure in the largest unit in which its size is at least 1, as `scaled` does. With `binary` true, data uses KiB through TiB.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the measure as its number and unit symbol, which is what `IO.printLine` and interpolation show. `inspected` and the REPL show the record's fields instead.

entries.name: scale
entries.summary:
Multiplies the measure by a plain number, keeping its unit.

Three times a two-second interval is six seconds, shown in seconds.

entries.name: raisedUnit
entries.summary: Returns this measure's unit raised to `exponent`, for `squared` and `cubed`: the factor raised to that power, a notation such as `m^2`, and the given dimension.

entries.name: convertTo
entries.summary:
Converts the measure to another unit of the same dimension.

Units from opt-in modules such as `Units.SI` and `Units.Data` work too. Converting to a unit of another dimension, such as seconds to meters, is an `Error`.

entries.name: convert
entries.summary: Converts the measure to another time unit; `convertTo` for time units only.

Adds two measures of the same dimension.

The units can differ. The sum is shown in the left operand's unit. Adding measures of different dimensions does not type-check.

Subtracts a measure of the same dimension.

As with +++, the result is shown in the left operand's unit.

entries.name: inOwnUnit
entries.summary: Returns a measure of `total` base units, shown in this measure's unit.

entries.name: scaledValue
entries.summary: Divides a canonical value by a unit factor. The conversion is exact in principle (0.000005 W is 5 μW), but neither number is exactly representable in binary, so the quotient can land an ulp or two off (5.000000000000001). Round back to 15 significant digits, comfortably inside a double's ~15.95, so converted measures read the way they were written.
Returns `true` when `other` is the same quantity of the same dimension.

entries.name: compare
entries.summary: Compares this quantity with `other`, a measure of the same dimension.
The ordering operators of `Comparable`, typed to take only a measure of the same dimension.

entries.name: Measure<Quantity.Length>
entries.summary: Powers of a length that have a dimension: `3.meter ^ 2` is an area and `2.meter ^ 3` a volume, the exponent literal choosing which. Other powers go through `pow` in `Units.Dynamic`, which checks them at run time.
Returns the length squared, the same as `squared`.

entries.name: squared
entries.summary: Returns the length squared, which is an area.

entries.name: cubed
entries.summary: Returns the length cubed, which is a volume and converts to litres.

entries.name: Units
entries.summary:
The time units under the `Units` name. They are also in the prelude.

`Units.Hour` and `Hour` are the same constructor: they match the same patterns and compare equal. The qualified name makes the unit family explicit.

```kex
90.minute.to(String, in: Units.Hour)   # => Just("1.5 h")
```

entries.name: URI
signatures: build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>

entries.name: URI
entries.summary:
Parses, builds and resolves URIs and URLs, and encodes query strings and HTML forms.

Parsing follows RFC 3986 strictly and keeps the text as it was written: `string` gives back the exact input. Normalizing is a separate step, done by `normalize` and `equivalent?`.

```kex
using URI

let base = URL.parse("https://example.test/a/").try
let reference = URI.parse("../items?limit=10").try
base.resolve(reference).try.string   # => "https://example.test/items?limit=10"
```

A parsed RFC 3986 URI reference: an absolute URI or a relative one.

Make one with `URI.parse` or `URI.fromIRI`, which check the syntax.

entries.name: URL
entries.summary:
An absolute URI with a host, such as an HTTP URL.

Every `URL` has a scheme and a host, so `scheme` and `host` return them directly, where the `URI` versions return optionals. Make one with `URL.parse` or `URL.build`.

entries.name: Host
entries.summary: A URI's host as written, in `display`, and in lowercase ASCII (IDNA) form, in `ascii`.

entries.name: Query
entries.summary:
The entries of a URI query string, in order.

Order and repeated keys are kept, since APIs rely on them: `tag=kex&tag=beam` has two entries. A value of `None` is a bare key, as in `?debug`; `Just("")` is a key with an empty value, as in `?debug=`.

entries.name: Form
entries.summary:
The fields of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, in order.

Forms encode a space as +++. In a `Query`, +++ is a literal plus sign.

entries.name: URIError
entries.summary: The error returned when a URI cannot be parsed, converted or resolved: its `kind`, and a message for a person to read.

entries.name: URIErrorKind
entries.summary: What kind of problem a `URIError` reports.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an RFC 3986 URI reference, which may be relative.

The text must be ASCII, with anything else already percent-encoded; use `URI.fromIRI` for text a person typed. Use `URL.parse` when the input must be a complete URL with a scheme and host.

entries.name: fromIRI
entries.summary:
Converts an internationalized address (an IRI) to an ASCII URI.

The host is converted with IDNA, and the rest of the non-ASCII text is percent-encoded as UTF-8. Use it for addresses people type or paste; `parse` rejects non-ASCII text.

entries.name: URI.URL
signatures: build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an absolute URL with a scheme and host.

A relative reference is a `NotAbsolute` error, and a URI without a host, such as `mailto:ada@example.com`, is `MissingAuthority`.

entries.name: build
signatures: build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>
entries.summary:
Builds a URL from a scheme, a host, path segments and a query.

Pass the path segments and query values unencoded. Each segment is encoded on its own, so a `/` inside a value stays part of that segment. The scheme and host are lowercased. The host must be ASCII: an international name has to be given in its `xn--` form.

entries.name: from
entries.summary:
Builds a query from a list of entries, keeping their order, repeated keys and bare keys.

A `None` value is encoded as a bare key, and `Just("")` as a key with an equals sign, so `?debug` and `?debug=` stay different.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses a query string, decoding percent escapes.

A +++ stays a plus sign; use `Form.parse` for form bodies, where it means a space.

entries.name: from
entries.summary: Builds a form from a list of fields, keeping their order and repeated names.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary: Parses an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, where +++ means a space.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the URI exactly as it was parsed.

entries.name: normalize
entries.summary:
Returns the URI in RFC 3986 normal form.

The scheme and host are lowercased, needless percent escapes are decoded, and `.` and `..` path segments are resolved. Parsing never does this by itself, because signatures, cache keys and logs may depend on the exact text.

entries.name: equivalent?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the two URIs are the same after normalizing.

`==` compares the text as written.

entries.name: resolve
entries.summary: Resolves `reference` against this URI, as a browser resolves a link against the page it is on.

entries.name: scheme
entries.summary: Returns the scheme in lowercase, or `None` for a relative reference.

entries.name: host
entries.summary: Returns the host, or `None` when the URI has none.

entries.name: query
entries.summary:
Returns the query, or `None` when the URI has no `?`.

A URI ending in a bare `?` has a query with no entries, which is not the same as `None`.

entries.name: showValue
entries.summary: Renders the URI with any password in it replaced by `***`.

entries.name: inspectValue
entries.summary: Renders the URI with any password in it replaced by `***`, as `showValue` does.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the URL exactly as it was parsed.

entries.name: normalize

entries.name: Control.Retry
signatures: run(operation: Block<X>, schedule: Schedule = …, attempts: Integer = …, delay: Duration = …, backoff: Float = …, maximumDelay: Duration = …, jitter: Float = …, maximumTotalDelay: Duration? = …, sleeper: (Duration -> Void) = …, random: Block<Float> = …, onRetry: (Info<X> -> Void) = …) -> X
entries.summary: Retries an operation that returns an error, with a delay between attempts.

entries.name: Control.Retry.Retry
signatures: run(operation: Block<X>, schedule: Schedule = …, attempts: Integer = …, delay: Duration = …, backoff: Float = …, maximumDelay: Duration = …, jitter: Float = …, maximumTotalDelay: Duration? = …, sleeper: (Duration -> Void) = …, random: Block<Float> = …, onRetry: (Info<X> -> Void) = …) -> X
entries.summary:
Running an operation until it succeeds or a `Schedule` runs out.

`run` calls the block at once. An `Ok` result is returned; an `Error` is retried after a wait, and when the schedule runs out the last error is returned as it is. To choose yourself what to retry, return `again` or `done` from the block.

An HTTP 429 or 503 response is `Ok(response)`, so retrying on a status needs `again`. Only retry a write when repeating it is harmless, for example with an idempotency key. The schedule limits the time spent sleeping, not the time spent in the operation, so give requests their own timeouts.

entries.name: Schedule
entries.summary:
The attempt limit and the waits `run` uses between attempts.

Every field has a default: three attempts, a first wait of 100 ms that doubles each time up to 5 seconds, and 20% jitter. A schedule only holds settings, so each `run` that uses it starts again from the first attempt.

entries.name: Decision
entries.summary:
A block's decision whether to retry, carrying its result.

From `run`, `Done(value)` means the block chose to stop, and `Again(value)` means it still wanted to retry when the schedule ran out. The value can be anything, including an `Error`.

entries.name: again
entries.summary: Returns `Again(value)`, asking `run` to try again if the schedule allows.

entries.name: done
entries.summary: Returns `Done(value)`, telling `run` to stop with `value`, whether that is a success or a failure not worth retrying.

entries.name: Info
entries.summary:
What `run` passes to `onRetry` just before it waits for the next attempt.

`onRetry` is called only when another attempt will follow, never after a success, a `done`, or the last attempt. The durations count sleep only, not time spent in the operation.

entries.name: run
signatures: run(operation: Block<X>, schedule: Schedule = …, attempts: Integer = …, delay: Duration = …, backoff: Float = …, maximumDelay: Duration = …, jitter: Float = …, maximumTotalDelay: Duration? = …, sleeper: (Duration -> Void) = …, random: Block<Float> = …, onRetry: (Info<X> -> Void) = …) -> X
entries.summary:
Calls `operation` until it succeeds, returns `done`, or runs out of attempts or sleep time, and returns its last result.

The first call happens at once, and each later one after a wait. Named timing options override that field of `schedule` for this run only.

When the block returns a `Result`, `Ok` stops and `Error` is retried. When it returns `done(value)` or `again(value)`, it decides itself. Use one of the two forms throughout the block. An error raised inside the block is not caught or retried.

Settings out of range are adjusted, not rejected: attempts below 1 become 1, negative durations zero, a backoff below 1 becomes 1, and jitter and the random samples are clamped to 0..1.

`Done(Error(...))` means the block gave up on an error not worth retrying. `Again(Ok(response))` means a response the block rejected, such as a 503, kept coming until the schedule ran out. `run` knows nothing about HTTP: deciding which statuses to retry and honouring `Retry-After` are up to the block.

`sleeper` and `random` are for tests, and replacing one leaves the other real. A sample of 0 picks the shortest jittered wait, 0.5 the unjittered one, and 1 the longest. With zero jitter `random` is not called. lint:allow parameter-count — named options make each setting independent

entries.summary:
A first-in-first-out queue.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Queue`.

```kex
using Data.Queue

let q = Queue.from([1, 2, 3])
q.enqueue(4).items    # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
q.peek                # => Just(1)
```

The queue is two lists. `front` holds the elements next in line, and `back` holds the newest ones in reverse. `enqueue` adds to the head of `back`, and `dequeue` takes the head of `front`, reversing `back` into `front` when `front` runs out. Both run in amortized constant time.

`items` gives the elements as a list, front first.

The same elements can be split between `front` and `back` in different ways: `Queue.from([1, 2])` and `Queue.from([1]).enqueue(2)` differ inside. `==` compares `items`, so it calls them equal. Map keys and record patterns compare the fields themselves, so to them the two queues differ.

Updates return a new queue. `enqueue!` and `dequeue!` rebind the variable instead.

Build one with `Queue.from` or `Queue.empty`.

entries.summary:
Immutable collections of distinct elements.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Set`, which brings in both kinds of set:

```kex
using Data.Set
```

Membership uses the same structural equality as `==` and map keys, so records and tuples are compared by value. Updates return a new set. The `!` forms (`add!`, `delete!`) rebind the variable they are called on to the new set.

```kex
let tags = Set.from(["kex", "beam", "kex"])
tags.count                     # => 2
tags.contains?("beam")         # => true
tags.add("erlang").items       # => ["beam", "erlang", "kex"]
```

The two kinds differ in how they store their elements:

```kex
Set           kept sorted, so iteration is in ascending order and the
              elements must be +Comparable+.
UnorderedSet  hash-based, so +contains?+ is a map lookup and the elements
              need only support equality. Iteration order is unspecified,
              so don't write a test that depends on it.
```

Use `Set` when you will read the elements back out, and `UnorderedSet` when the set is mostly asked `contains?`.

Two sets are equal when they have the same elements. `items` returns the elements as a list, in no particular order for an `UnorderedSet`.

entries.name: Set
entries.summary:
A set whose elements are kept sorted and free of duplicates.

Build one with `Set.from`. A `Set { items: ... }` literal neither sorts nor removes duplicates, and every function here assumes both. `items` is the stored list, so reading it costs nothing.

```kex
Set.from([3, 1, 2]).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

entries.name: UnorderedSet
entries.summary:
A set stored as a map from each element to `true`.

Build one with `UnorderedSet.from`. Iteration follows the map's internal order, so use `items.sort` when you need a stable order.

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([3, 1, 2]).contains?(2)   # => true
```

entries.summary:
A last-in-first-out stack.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Stack`.

```kex
using Data.Stack
```

`push`, `pop` and `peek` take constant time. `items` lists the elements bottom to top, the order they were pushed in:

```kex
let s = Stack.from([1, 2, 3])
s.peek                                         # => Just(3)
s.push(4).items                                # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
s.pop.map { |top, rest| (top, rest.items) }    # => Just((3, [1, 2]))
Stack.empty.pop                                # => None
```

Every update returns a new stack. `push!` rebinds the variable to the result, as `add!` does for `Data.Set`.

entries.name: Stack
entries.summary:
A stack of elements.

Build one with `Stack.from`. The record literal takes its elements top first, the reverse of `items`.

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

entries.name: Kex.AST
signatures: parse(source: String, filename: String) -> Result<Program, ParseError>
entries.summary:
Parses Kex source code into a structured AST, at run time.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Kex.AST`.

Use it to write tools that read Kex source, such as linters, formatters, documentation generators and code search. The AST covers modules, function signatures, types and records, traits, make blocks, and the doc comments attached to them; `tey docs` builds the standard library's reference from it.

```kex
using Kex.AST

main do
  match Kex.AST.parseFile("src/main.kex") do
    Ok(program) => IO.printLine("${program.items.count} top-level items")
    Error(e)    => IO.printError(e.message)
  end
end
```

The parsing functions return a `Result`, with a `ParseError` when the source does not parse.

entries.name: Location
entries.summary:
Where in a source file something appeared.

Line and column are 1-based, for messages to a person. The offsets are 0-based byte positions, for slicing the source.

entries.name: Program
entries.summary: A parsed source file: its schema version, and its top-level items.

entries.name: ParseError
entries.summary: Why a source file could not be parsed.

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(source: String, filename: String) -> Result<Program, ParseError>
entries.summary:
Parses Kex source text into a structured AST.

Pass `filename` when you have one; it is recorded in every `Location`, including the one in a `ParseError`.

entries.name: parseFile
entries.summary:
Reads a file and parses it, reporting locations against its path.

A file that cannot be read also gives an `Error`, with no location.

entries.name: parseType
entries.summary:
Parses a type expression on its own, without a surrounding program.

Use it for a type that arrives as text, such as a signature in a config file or a type named on the command line. `typeRefText` renders the result back.

entries.name: parseExpression
entries.summary:
Parses a single expression on its own, without a surrounding program.

This gives the expression's structure. To evaluate it, use `Evaluator.runExpression`.

entries.name: SyntaxToken
entries.summary:
One token of a lossless syntax tree, exactly as written.

`parseSyntax` keeps everything `parse` drops, such as spacing and comments, so `toSource` reprints the file byte for byte. Use it to build a formatter, or a linter that rewrites code.

entries.name: SyntaxElement
entries.summary: One child of a `SyntaxNode`: a token, or a nested node.

entries.name: SyntaxNode
entries.summary:
A declaration, expression, pattern or type, holding its own tokens and nested nodes in source order.

```kex
let tree = Kex.AST.parseSyntax("# the answer\nlet x = 42\n").try
tree.kind                  # => "Program"
Kex.AST.toSource(tree)     # => "# the answer\nlet x = 42\n"
```

entries.name: parseSyntax
entries.summary: Parses Kex source into its lossless syntax tree.

entries.name: toSource
entries.summary:
Reprints a syntax tree as the source it was parsed from, byte for byte.

Each node prints its own tokens and nested nodes in order; nothing is copied from the original text. A rearranged tree therefore prints the rearranged program, with comments moved along with their code.

entries.name: elementSource
entries.summary: Returns the source of one child of a node: a token's trivia and text, or a nested node reprinted.

entries.name: commentsBefore
entries.summary:
Returns the comments on their own lines directly above the child at `index`. These belong to the child: a formatter moves them with it, and a `# kex:disable-next-line` among them applies to it.

A comment at the end of the previous line belongs to that line and is not included.

entries.name: blankLinesBefore
entries.summary: Returns how many blank lines separate the child at `index` from what precedes it.

entries.name: linesBefore
entries.summary: Returns the whole lines between the child at `index` and the code before it, taken from the trivia of the `Newline` tokens that end them. The newline ending the previous line of code is not included, since what sits in front of it belongs to that code.

entries.name: TypeRef
entries.summary:
A type as it was written in source.

`typeRefText` renders one back to the source spelling.

entries.name: typeRefText
entries.summary:
Renders a `TypeRef` back to the way it is written in source.

A list reads as `[Integer]`, a map as `{String: Integer}` and an optional as `String?`.

entries.name: PatternRef
entries.summary:
A pattern as it was written in source.

Pattern nodes describe what a function clause or match arm accepts. A linter can tell a wildcard from a binding, for example, without reparsing the text.

entries.name: PatternField
entries.summary:
One field inside a record or map-shaped pattern.

`pattern` is `None` for shorthand such as `{ name }`. `stringKey?` is `true` for the string-key spelling `{"name": value}` and `false` for the atom-key `{ name: value }`.

entries.name: patternRefText
entries.summary: Renders a `PatternRef` back to the way it is written in source.

entries.name: referenceText
entries.summary:
Renders either a type or a pattern back to source.

Use it when a node may hold either kind; it calls `typeRefText` or `patternRefText` as needed.

entries.name: Expression
entries.summary:
An expression as it was written in source.

Expressions keep the syntax distinctions tools care about: a call with a receiver is its own node, `var` is distinct from `let`, and a trailing `if` can be told apart from a block `if`. To run an expression, use `Evaluator`.

entries.name: NamedArgument
entries.summary: One `name: value` argument at a call site.

entries.name: MatchArm
entries.summary:
One arm of `match`, `receive`, or `rescue`.

Multiple `patterns` are the comma-separated alternatives on the left of the arrow. `guard` is absent when the arm has no `when` condition.

entries.name: LambdaParam
entries.summary: One lambda parameter and its optional source annotation.

entries.name: RescueInfo
entries.summary:
The structured recovery clauses attached to a function or expression.

Rescue arms with patterns are in `arms`. A catch-all rescue has its optional binding and its body in separate fields. `inlineReturn` holds the value of the compact `rescue return X` form.

entries.name: ElseIf
entries.summary: One `elif` branch, in source order.

entries.name: MapItem
entries.summary: One entry in a map literal: either a key/value pair or `...spread`.

entries.name: RecordField

entries.name: GeneratedTemplate
entries.summary:
A declaration template whose name, or for a make block its target, is computed by a `compiled do` expression.

It appears only in code that generates declarations. After expansion, the generated declarations are ordinary +Node+s.

entries.name: GeneratedMakeInfo
entries.summary: The fixed portion of a generated `make` declaration.

entries.name: MainInfo
entries.summary: The program entry point, including documentation and recovery clauses.

entries.name: ParamInfo
entries.summary:
One declared function parameter.

`name` is `None` for a destructuring parameter, whose shape is in `pattern`. `default?` is `true` when the parameter has a default value.

entries.name: ClauseInfo
entries.summary:
One clause of a function, including its patterns and body.

All clauses of a function are in one `FunctionInfo`, in source order, which is the order their patterns are tried in.

entries.name: FunctionInfo
entries.summary:
A named function and all of its pattern-matching clauses.

`doc` holds the doc comment directly above the declaration, without its `#` markers, or `None` when there is none.

entries.name: AnnotationInfo
entries.summary:
A standalone function type signature.

`implicitThis?` is `true` for a receiver signature written with `:>`, and `false` for a module-level signature written with `:`.

entries.name: VariantInfo

entries.name: TypeInfo
entries.summary:
A type alias or algebraic data type declaration.

`variants` is set for an algebraic data type and `None` for an alias or an abstract type. `parents` lists the declared bounds and parent types.

entries.name: FieldInfo
entries.summary: One field declared by a record type.

entries.name: RecordInfo
entries.summary: A record declaration with fields in source order.

entries.name: TraitInfo
entries.summary: A trait declaration and the signatures or default functions in its body.

A `make` implementation block.

`target` is the receiver type and `implements` lists the traits named in `implement:`. `body` holds the functions and visibility sections in declaration order.

entries.name: Net.DNS
signatures: lookup(kind: RecordType, name: Name) -> Result<LookupResponse, NetError>
entries.summary:
DNS lookups, with resolvers that own a bounded cache.

Use `DNS.addresses` for an occasional lookup. Open a `Resolver` when a service looks names up repeatedly, wants cache statistics or must query a particular nameserver; the cache lives in the resolver and is freed when you close it. On the interpreter (`kex -R`), lookups work only through a mock.

```kex
using Net.DNS

let resolver = Resolver.system.try
let name = Name.parse("example.test").try
let addresses = resolver.addresses(name).try
resolver.close
```

entries.name: Name
entries.summary:
A validated DNS name, in the caller's spelling and in IDNA ASCII.

`display` is the name as the caller wrote it, for messages. `ascii` is the IDNA form sent in queries.

entries.name: RecordType
entries.summary: The record types `Resolver.lookup` can ask for.

entries.name: DNSSECStatus
entries.summary: The DNSSEC state the system resolver reported. Kex does not validate DNSSEC itself, so this is often `Indeterminate`.

entries.name: DNSRecord

entries.name: LookupResponse

entries.name: CacheOptions
entries.summary:
Limits for a resolver's cache.

`entries` caps the number of cached names. An answer is kept for its DNS TTL, but no longer than `maximumTtl`. A failed lookup is kept for `negativeTtl`, so a missing hostname is not sent to the nameserver on every request.

entries.name: Nameserver
entries.summary: A DNS server for `Resolver.custom` to query.

entries.name: ResolverOptions
entries.summary:
Settings for `Resolver.custom`.

With an empty `search` list only the name as written is queried. Otherwise the search domains are tried in order for a name with a single label. `retries` and `timeout` apply to each query.

entries.name: CacheStatistics
entries.summary:
A resolver's cache counters, counted since it was opened. `entries` is the current number of cached names; `clear` resets it but not the counters.

Compare `hits` with `misses` when tuning `CacheOptions`. A rising `evictions` count means the resolver sees more distinct names than its cache holds.

entries.name: Net.IP
entries.summary:
IP addresses and CIDR networks, checked and stored in canonical form.

```kex
using Net.IP

let address = Address.parse("192.0.2.42").try
let network = Network.parse("192.0.2.0/24").try
network.contains?(address)   # => true
```

entries.name: Address
entries.summary:
An IPv4 or IPv6 address.

The text is stored in canonical form, so two spellings of the same address compare equal and print the same. `Address.parse` rejects zone identifiers such as `%en0`.

entries.name: Network
entries.summary:
A CIDR network, stored with its host bits cleared.

Parsing `192.0.2.9/24` gives `192.0.2.0/24`, so two spellings of the same range are equal.

entries.name: Net.IP.Address
entries.summary: Parsing IP addresses.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Invalid text is a `NetError` of kind `Parse`.

IPv4 must be a dotted quad of exactly four decimal octets, each 0 to 255 with no leading zero. The shorthand and legacy spellings some resolvers accept, `127.1`, `1`, `0x7f.0.0.1` and the octal `010.0.0.1`, are rejected, so an address checked against an allow-list is the address used. IPv6 may end in such a dotted quad (`::ffff:192.0.2.1`); a zone identifier such as `%en0` is rejected. Surrounding spaces are rejected.

entries.name: Net.IP.Network
entries.summary: Parsing CIDR networks.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses an address and prefix length such as `192.0.2.0/24`, clearing the host bits. Invalid text is a `NetError` of kind `Parse`.

The address takes the same syntax as `Address.parse`. The prefix length is plain decimal, at most 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6; a sign, a space or a leading zero, as in `/024`, is rejected.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the canonical text form of the address.

entries.name: version
entries.summary: Returns the address family as `4` or `6`.

entries.name: loopback?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a loopback address: anything in `127.0.0.0/8`, or `::1`.

entries.name: private?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for an address reserved for private networks.

A private address can still belong to another machine, so it does not prove that a peer is trusted.

entries.name: unspecified?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for the all-zero address: `0.0.0.0` or `::`.

On a listening endpoint it usually means all local interfaces. It cannot be used as a remote destination.

entries.name: multicast?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the address names a multicast group.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the canonical CIDR text, including the prefix length.

entries.name: contains?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `address` falls within this network.

An address of the other IP version is never inside, so there is no need to compare `version` first.

entries.name: prefix
entries.summary: Returns the number of fixed leading address bits.

entries.name: first
entries.summary: Returns the first address in the range, with all host bits cleared.

entries.name: last
entries.summary: Returns the last address in the range, with all host bits set. For IPv4 this is the broadcast address, which is usually not assignable to a host.

entries.summary:
TCP, UDP and Unix-domain sockets, and TLS client connections.

Every socket is owned by a process of its own. Functions that can fail return a `NetError`, and closing a socket twice is harmless. Without a timeout argument, accepting and receiving give up after 30 seconds with a `Timeout` error.

Sockets work on BEAM only. On the tree-walking interpreter every operation returns an `UnsupportedBackend` error unless the capability is replaced with a mock such as `Mock.TCP`.

```kex
using Net
using Net.Socket

let listener = TCP.listen(TCP.Endpoint.loopback(Port.from(0).try)).try
let address = listener.localAddress.try
let client = TCP.connect(address).try
client.sendAll("ping".to(Binary).try).try
listener.close
```

entries.name: Net.Socket.Mock
entries.summary:
Stand-ins for the socket capabilities, for testing how code handles a failure.

They are here, not in `mock.kex`, because only code compiled together with this module can implement its capabilities.

entries.name: TCP
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `Net.Socket.TCP` capability.

Every function that would open a connection or listener returns `failure` when it is set, so a test can force a refused connection or a timeout. Otherwise they, and every function on a connection, return a `MockEmpty` error. The mock cannot make a working connection; test that path against a loopback listener (see `spec/net_socket_text_beam.kex`).

```kex
with Net.Socket.TCP = Mock.TCP {} do
  TCP.connectTo("127.0.0.1:9")
end
```

```kex
  UDP.bindTo("127.0.0.1:0")
end
```

entries.name: Net.HTTP.WebSocket
signatures: connect(url: String, options: ClientOptions) -> Result<Connection, NetError>
entries.summary:
WebSocket (RFC 6455) connections that send and receive whole messages.

A `Connection` reassembles fragmented messages and answers pings itself. It does not reconnect or send heartbeats: what a dropped connection means, such as having to subscribe again or resume from a cursor, is up to your program.

```kex
using Net.HTTP.WebSocket

let socket = WebSocket.connect("wss://example.test/events").try
socket.send(Text("hello")).try
let message = socket.receiveMessage.try
socket.close
```

entries.name: Message
entries.summary:
One complete WebSocket message.

`CloseMessage` carries the peer's status code and reason. It ends the message stream, whatever the code, and later reads fail with `Closed`.

entries.name: ClientOptions
entries.summary:
Options for a client connection: the subprotocols to offer and the largest message to accept.

List `subprotocols` in order of preference. `maximumMessageBytes` (16 MiB by default) applies to a whole reassembled message, so many small fragments cannot get around it; a larger incoming message is a `Limit` error. It also caps what `send` accepts.

entries.name: Session
entries.summary: What the handshake settled. `subprotocol` is `None` when none was chosen.

entries.name: Connection
entries.summary: An open WebSocket connection, on the client or the server side. It does not reconnect on its own.

entries.name: Handshake
entries.summary: The subprotocols an incoming upgrade request offers, in the order the client listed them.

entries.name: Upgrade
entries.summary:
A server's answer to a `Handshake`.

`Accept(handler, headers, subprotocol)` sends the 101 response and then runs `handler` with the server `Connection`; its return value is ignored. The `headers` are added to the 101 response, except `Upgrade`, `Connection`, `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` and `Content-Length`, which are dropped. `subprotocol` must be one the client offered, or `None`; choosing any other makes the server answer 500.

`Reject(response)` sends `response` as a plain HTTP response, such as `Response.text(426, "chat.v2 required")` for a client that lacks a subprotocol you need.

entries.name: Net.HTTP.WebSocket.WebSocket
signatures: connect(url: String, options: ClientOptions) -> Result<Connection, NetError>
entries.summary: Opening client connections and accepting server ones.

entries.name: connect
signatures: connect(url: String, options: ClientOptions) -> Result<Connection, NetError>
entries.summary:
Opens a client connection to a `ws:` or `wss:` URL with default options.

A `wss:` connection verifies the server's certificate. The handshake gives up with a `Timeout` error after about 11 seconds.

entries.name: upgrade
entries.summary:
Answers a WebSocket upgrade request in a `Net.HTTP.Server` route handler.

Return the result from the handler as it is. `decide` is called only for a valid handshake. A request that is not one gets 400 Bad Request (wrong method, a missing or malformed `Sec-WebSocket-Key`), or 426 Upgrade Required when the `Sec-WebSocket-Version` is not 13.

entries.name: send
entries.summary:
Sends one text, binary or close message.

Text that is not valid UTF-8, a message over the size limit and an invalid close code are `Protocol` errors. Sending on a closed connection is a `Closed` error. On a client connection any failed send also closes the connection.

entries.name: receiveMessage
entries.summary:
Waits for the next message and returns it, for as long as the peer stays connected.

Fragments are joined and pings answered along the way. Text that is not valid UTF-8 is a `Protocol` error, and a message over the size limit a `Limit` error. The peer's `CloseMessage` is returned once; reads after it fail with `Closed`, as do reads after the connection drops.

entries.name: session
entries.summary: Returns what the handshake settled, such as the chosen subprotocol.

entries.name: close
entries.summary:
Sends a normal close frame (code 1000) and closes the connection.

Closing an already closed connection does nothing. To give the peer a different code or a reason, `send` a `CloseMessage` first.

entries.name: closed?
entries.summary:
Returns whether the connection is closed.

A server connection counts as closed as soon as either side closes it or the transport fails. A client connection counts as closed once it has finished shutting down.

entries.name: Units.Data
signatures: to(String: Type, in: DataUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
convertTo(measure: Measure<D>, unit: DataUnit) -> Result<Measure<D>, String>
entries.summary:
Data sizes: bytes, kilobytes, and their binary counterparts.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Units.Data`.

```kex
using Units.Data

main do
  IO.printLine(1500.megabyte.to(String))              # prints: 1500.0 MB
  IO.printLine(1500000000.byte.to(String, in: GB).or("")) # prints: 1.5 GB
end
```

There are two families of units: `KB` is 1000 bytes and `KiB` is 1024. Every size is counted in bytes, so the two convert into each other: `1.gibibyte.convertTo(MiB)` gives 1024 MiB.

The constructors have singular names, as in `Units.SI`: `5.megabyte`, `2.mebibyte`. `byteSize` is another name for `byte`.

File and payload functions return plain integer byte counts. Wrap a count with `byte` to convert or display it:

```kex
FS.File.size("report.pdf").map { |n| n.byte.showValue }
Binary.fromBytes([104, 105]).length.byte.to(String)  # => Just("2.0 B")
"é".bytes.count.byte.to(String)                    # => Just("2.0 B")
```

To display a size in a particular unit, name the unit:

```kex
1048576.byte.to(String, in: MiB)                           # => Just("1.0 MiB")
4312.byte.to(String, in: KB, format: Number.format`#.#`)   # => Just("4.3 KB")
1048576.byte.convertTo(MiB).map { |m| m.showValue }        # => Ok("1.0 MiB")
```

An integer byte count compares directly with a data size:

```kex
30000001 > 30.megabyte   # => true
1048576 <= 1.mebibyte    # => true
```

`<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` work with the count on either side. Comparing a count with a measure that is not a data size, such as a time, fails an assertion.

Every size is a prelude `Measure`, so measure arithmetic and `to(String)` work on it.

entries.name: DataUnit
entries.summary:
The data units: decimal (`KB`, `MB`, `GB`, `TB`), binary (`KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB`), and the byte `B`. A size's `canonical` value is in bytes.

```kex
size(1, KB).canonical    # => 1000.0
size(1, KiB).canonical   # => 1024.0
```

entries.name: Measure
signatures: to(String: Type, in: DataUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary: Adds `to(String, in:)` for this module's units, to display a size in a chosen data unit.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(String: Type, in: DataUnit, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary:
Renders a size in the given data unit, decimal or binary.

A measure that is not a data size gives `None`.

entries.name: size
entries.summary:
Returns a size of `value` in the given data unit.

Use it when the unit is chosen at run time. When it is known in the code, `megabyte`, `kibibyte` and the other named constructors read better.

entries.name: convertTo
signatures: convertTo(measure: Measure<D>, unit: DataUnit) -> Result<Measure<D>, String>
entries.summary:
Converts a size to another data unit.

Decimal and binary units convert into each other. A measure that is not a data size, such as a time, gives an `Error`.

entries.name: byteSize
entries.summary:
Returns a size of `value` bytes; the same as `byte`.

It is not called `bytes` because `String.bytes` already gives a string's UTF-8 encoding.

entries.name: byte
entries.summary:
Returns a size of `value` bytes.

Use it to wrap byte counts from `FS.File.size` or `Binary.length`.

entries.name: kilobyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` kilobytes, 1000 bytes each.

entries.name: megabyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` megabytes, 1000000 bytes each.

entries.name: gigabyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` gigabytes, 10^9 bytes each.

entries.name: terabyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` terabytes, 10^12 bytes each.

entries.name: kibibyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` kibibytes, 1024 bytes each.

entries.name: mebibyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` mebibytes, 1024^2 bytes each.

entries.name: gibibyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` gibibytes, 1024^3 bytes each.

entries.name: tebibyte
entries.summary: Returns a size of `value` tebibytes, 1024^4 bytes each.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
Lets an integer byte count be compared with a data size.

File and binary sizes are plain integers; with this module imported they compare directly against sizes such as `30.megabyte`. A measure that is not a data size fails an assertion.

entries.name: Units.Dynamic
signatures: unit(scale: Float, dimension: Dimension, notation: String) -> Result<DynamicUnit, UnitError>
scaled(factor: Float, notation: String) -> Result<DynamicUnit, UnitError>
entries.summary:
Quantities whose units are built at run time.

`Measure` (units.kex) checks dimensions at compile time. Here a unit is a value: a scale to its dimension's canonical unit, a `Dimension` and a notation. Arithmetic checks dimensions when it runs and returns a `Result`, with `DimensionMismatch` when they do not agree.

```kex
let meters = unit(1.0, Dimensions.base(Length {}), "m").try
let seconds = unit(1.0, Dimensions.base(Time {}), "s").try
let kilometers = meters.scaled(1000.0, "km").try
let hours = seconds.scaled(3600.0, "h").try
let speed = (measure(36.0, kilometers) / measure(1.0, hours)).try
speed.convertTo((meters / seconds).try).try.value   # => 10.0
speed.convertTo(meters).ok?                         # => false
```

entries.name: unit
signatures: unit(scale: Float, dimension: Dimension, notation: String) -> Result<DynamicUnit, UnitError>
entries.summary:
Returns a unit that is `scale` times the canonical unit of `dimension`.

`scale` must be positive and finite; otherwise the result is `InvalidScale`.

entries.name: measure
entries.summary: Returns `value` of `unit`. The unit is kept for display, and the quantity is stored in the canonical unit.

entries.name: DynamicUnit
signatures: scaled(factor: Float, notation: String) -> Result<DynamicUnit, UnitError>

entries.summary: Returns the product of two units. The notation keeps the grouping, as in `"(m)·(s)"`. The result is `ScaleOverflow` when the scales overflow and `InvalidScale` when they underflow.

entries.name: scaled
signatures: scaled(factor: Float, notation: String) -> Result<DynamicUnit, UnitError>

entries.name: value
entries.summary: Returns the quantity's magnitude in its display unit.

entries.name: compareTo
entries.summary: Orders two quantities of the same dimension, whatever their display units. Quantities of different dimensions give `DimensionMismatch`.

entries.name: Units.SI
signatures: to(String: Type, in: SIPrefix, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
rescaled(factor: Float, kind: Atom, symbol: String) -> This?
entries.summary:
SI units such as metres, grams, watts and volts, with prefixes and dimensional arithmetic.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Units.SI`.

```kex
using Units.SI

main do
  IO.printLine(3.kilowatt.to(String))           # prints: 3.0 kW
  IO.printLine(5000.meter.to(String, in: Kilo(Meter)).or("")) # prints: 5.0 km
  IO.printLine((100.meter / 10.second).to(String)) # prints: 10.0 m/s
end
```

Every value is a prelude `Measure`, with its arithmetic, conversion and comparison. This module adds the SI unit names, including prefixed ones such as `kilometer`; the prefixes as units (`Kilo(Meter)`) for `convertTo` and `to(String, in:)`; and the dimension of each product and quotient, so `2.newton * 3.meter` is in joules and `100.meter / 10.second` in metres per second.

entries.name: SIUnit
entries.summary:
The SI units this module names.

Each has a dimension (`:length`, `:mass`, `:power`, ...) and the symbol a `Measure` in it displays with.

entries.name: SIPrefix
entries.summary:
A decimal prefix applied to a unit, which makes another unit.

`Kilo(Meter)` is the kilometre and `Kilo(Watt * Hour)` the kilowatt-hour. Use one as the target of `convertTo` or `to(String, in:)`. To write a measure in a prefixed unit, use the prefixed name: `5.kilometer`.

```kex
5000.meter.convertTo(Kilo(Meter)).map(&.showValue)   # => Ok("5.0 km")
1500.watt.to(String, in: Kilo(Watt))    # => Just("1.5 kW")
```

entries.name: Measure
signatures: to(String: Type, in: SIPrefix, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
rescaled(factor: Float, kind: Atom, symbol: String) -> This?
entries.summary: Displays a measure in a prefixed unit, as the prelude's `to(String, in:)` does for other units.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(String: Type, in: SIPrefix, format: NumberFormat) -> String?
entries.summary:
Renders the measure in a prefixed unit.

Returns `None` when the unit has a different dimension from the measure, such as watts shown in metres.

entries.name: rescaled
signatures: rescaled(factor: Float, kind: Atom, symbol: String) -> This?
entries.summary: The measure in a unit of `factor`, or None across dimensions.

entries.name: prefixScaled
entries.summary: Divides the canonical value by a prefix factor. The conversion is exact in principle (0.000005 W is 5 μW) but neither the measured value nor the prefix factor is exactly representable in binary, so the quotient lands an ulp or two off (5.000000000000001). Round back to 15 significant digits, comfortably inside a double's ~15.95, so prefixed measures read the way they were written.

entries.name: meter
entries.summary: Returns `value` metres as a `Measure`.

entries.name: gram
entries.summary: Returns `value` grams as a `Measure`.

entries.name: kelvin
entries.summary: Returns `value` kelvin as a `Measure`.

entries.name: liter
entries.summary: Returns `value` litres as a `Measure`.

entries.name: newton
entries.summary: Returns `value` newtons as a `Measure`.

entries.name: joule
entries.summary: Returns `value` joules as a `Measure`.

entries.name: watt
entries.summary: Returns `value` watts as a `Measure`.

entries.name: volt
entries.summary: Returns `value` volts as a `Measure`.

entries.name: ampere
entries.summary: Returns `value` amperes as a `Measure`.

entries.name: ohm
entries.summary: Returns `value` ohms as a `Measure`.

entries.name: coulomb
entries.summary: Returns `value` coulombs as a `Measure`.

entries.name: Measure<Quantity.Mass>
entries.summary:
Products and quotients of measures, by dimension.

Each is declared with the dimension of its result, so the checker knows that `2.newton * 3.meter` is a `Measure<Quantity.Energy>`. A product with no dimension declared here, such as `2.meter * 3.second`, is a type error. `times` and `per` are the named forms of `*` and `/`. A dimension of your own declares its products the same way, in its own module.

entries.name: Grants
answered
entries.summary:
Carries out one request line and returns the response line.

It does not fail: a request that cannot be parsed, or is not allowed, gets an `{"ok":false}` response that says why.

entries.name: host
entries.summary:
Returns the lower-cased host name of an `http` or `https` URL.

Any other scheme is an error, and so is a URL with user information before the host (`https://user@host/`), which could disguise the real host.

entries.name: root
entries.summary: Returns the cache directory: `TEY_CACHE`, or `~/.cache/tey`, or `.tey-cache` when `HOME` is not set.

entries.name: packagePath
entries.summary:
Returns where a dependency's package lives in the cache.

A Git checkout is stored under a hash of its URL and then its commit, so two packages with the same name from different sources never share one. A `path` dependency's location comes from `Tey.Snapshot`.

entries.name: fetch
entries.summary:
Makes sure a dependency is in the cache, cloning it at its locked commit if needed, and returns its package path.

A workspace package is an error, since it is never cached.

entries.name: verify
entries.summary:
Checks that a cached dependency matches the SHA-256 in the lockfile, and returns its package path.

It is an error when the dependency is not cached, or when `git archive` of its commit hashes to something else.

entries.name: parser
entries.summary:
Returns Tey's built-in options and commands as one `OptionConfig`.

`OptionParser` matches the command words, removes them, and passes the rest to the handler. The help text and the dispatch come from this one list, so they cannot disagree.

entries.name: cli
entries.summary:
Returns the parser Tey runs: `parser` plus one command for each `command(...)` in the current package's manifest.

Because they are declared like the built-ins, package commands appear in `tey help` and in the unknown-command message. They cannot shadow a built-in, since the manifest reader rejects those names (`Tey.Manifest.reservedCommands`), and they are listed under their own "Package commands" heading so a reader knows to look in package.kex.

entries.name: dispatch
entries.summary:
Runs the Tey command line `args` and returns the exit code.

The color flags are handled first, by setting `NO_COLOR`. The line is then parsed once to answer what `run` cannot, namely whether it asks for `--version` and whether it names a built-in command, and handed to `run`, which parses it again and dispatches. A parse error is left for `run` to report with the help text.

entries.name: colorFlag?
entries.summary:
Returns whether `argument` turns colors off.

Both `--no-color` and `--no-colors`, the spelling `kex` uses, are accepted.

entries.name: plain?
entries.summary:
Returns whether `args` asks for output without colors.

Only arguments before a bare `--` count; those after it belong to the program being run, which may have a `--no-color` of its own.

entries.name: withoutColorFlags
entries.summary:
Returns `args` without the color flags before any bare `--`.

`dispatch` handles those flags itself by setting `NO_COLOR`, which `Console`, every child `kex` and the parser's error text all read. Removing them here makes the flag work anywhere on the line, including after `tey docs`, whose own parser does not know it.

entries.name: relayColors
entries.summary:
Sets `FORCE_COLOR` so every `kex` that Tey starts uses colors when Tey does.

It does nothing when colors are off or `NO_COLOR` is set, so `NO_COLOR` still wins in every child. `Kex.AST` passes `--no-colors`, which overrides this, so output Tey parses back has no escape codes.

entries.name: announceToolchain
entries.summary:
Sets `KEX` to the compiler Tey selected, so the rest of the process uses it.

`Kex.AST`, which reads `package.kex`, runs the compiler named by `KEX` and otherwise whatever `kex` is on PATH. Tey is started by `erl`, not by `kex`, so without this a manifest would be read by an unrelated compiler, or by none when `kex` lives only inside the Tey home. A `KEX` that is already set is left alone.

entries.name: install
entries.summary:
`tey install` in a package: installs its dependencies, then its targets.

`--without dev` skips fetching a group's dependencies. The lockfile still lists them, so dropping the flag later needs no new resolve.

entries.name: installWorkspace
signatures: installWorkspace(without: String, packageName: String, force?: Bool, approveAll?: Bool) -> Integer
entries.summary: Does what `install` does. `force?` lets targets replace programs Tey does not own (see `Tey.Programs.refusal`), and `approveAll?` approves every plugin without asking.

entries.name: installDependencies
signatures: installDependencies(context: Context, without: String, approveAll?: Bool) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Does everything `tey install` does before building: resolves the workspace's lock or reuses it, fetches and verifies what it names, approves plugins, and writes the lock.

entries.name: installPrograms
entries.summary: `tey install <argument>...`: installs a program from a path or a Git URL, or updates installed programs by name. Several arguments must all be names, since a source is one program with its own options.

entries.name: reinstallProgram
entries.summary:
`tey install <name>`: updates an installed program by installing it again from the source its receipt records.

A tag or an exact commit stays pinned unless a new `--tag`, `--branch` or `--ref` is given. A branch, HEAD or path is rebuilt only when its commit or content changed, unless `--rebuild` asks for it, say after an Erlang upgrade or a compiler fix.

entries.name: uninstallPrograms
entries.summary: `tey uninstall <name>...`: removes the programs each receipt owns, then the receipt and its build tree. A program since replaced by a file Tey did not write is left in place, with a message.

entries.name: installFromPath
entries.summary: Installs the program at `path` without writing to it. The workspace around it is copied to a staging directory, which gets its own lock, dependencies and build, and replaces the program's previous build tree only once its programs are installed. The checkout gains no `ebin/` and no `tey.lock`.

entries.name: installFromGit
entries.summary: Installs a program from a Git repository, at the commit `--tag`, `--branch` or `--ref` names, or at the default branch's HEAD. The commit is fetched into the cache like a dependency and installed from there like a path, so nothing is built inside the cache.

entries.name: previousApprovals
entries.summary: Returns the plugin approvals recorded in the lock of program `name`'s previous install, or none for a first install.

entries.name: programMember
signatures: programMember(context: Context, packageName: String) -> Result<Member, String>
entries.summary: Returns the workspace member a program install is for: the one `--package` names, or else the one the path is inside.

entries.name: installProgramMember
signatures: installProgramMember(context: Context, member: Member, options: InstallOptions, origin: Receipt) -> Integer
entries.summary: Finishes a path or Git install once the member is known: refuses a library, checks `--target`, then stages, builds and installs the programs.

entries.name: installStaged
signatures: installStaged(context: Context, member: Member, staging: String, options: InstallOptions, origin: Receipt) -> Integer

entries.name: dependencyClosure
entries.summary: Returns `roots` and every package they depend on, directly or not, in the newly resolved graph: the names an update affects.

entries.name: mergeUpdate
signatures: mergeUpdate(previous: LockState, fresh: LockState, roots: [String], wholeWorkspace?: Bool) -> LockState
entries.summary: Returns the lock after an update: the fresh workspace data and the fresh resolutions for `roots` and what they depend on, with every other external pin kept as it was. With `wholeWorkspace?` everything is fresh. Existing approvals are carried over; `approvePlugins` later drops those that no longer match a declaration.

entries.name: lockReusable?
signatures: lockReusable?(state: LockState, manifestFingerprint: String, toolchain: Tey.Toolchain.ToolchainInfo) -> Bool

entries.name: installTargetsSelected
signatures: installTargetsSelected(context: Context, packageName: String, force?: Bool = …) -> Integer

entries.name: installMemberTargets
entries.summary:
Installs the package's `target(...)` executables into `${TEY_HOME}/bin`, beside the `kex` shim, and records them in the package's receipt (see `Tey.Programs`). That directory is already on PATH for anyone who set up Tey.

A package without targets, such as a library, is left alone. Every name is checked before anything is built, so a refused install changes nothing.

entries.name: installMemberTargetsFrom
signatures: installMemberTargetsFrom(member: Member, force?: Bool, origin: Receipt, selected: [String]) -> Integer
entries.summary:
Does what `installMemberTargets` does, but records `origin`'s source in the receipt, since a program built in a staging copy came from somewhere else.

`selected` limits the targets installed (`--target`); empty means all.

entries.name: releaseTarget
signatures: releaseTarget(owner: String, name: String) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Removes `name` from `owner`'s receipt after another package took it over with `--force`. A receipt left owning nothing is deleted.

entries.name: recordInstall
signatures: recordInstall(package: ManifestPackage, origin: Receipt, installed: [String], receipts: [Receipt], claims: [(String, Claim)]) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Writes the package's receipt. Names taken over with `--force` are removed from the other package's receipt, and targets the previous receipt owned but this install no longer declares are deleted from the bin directory.

entries.name: dependencyRoots
entries.summary: Returns a `--source-root` for every fetched dependency of the workspace around the working directory, so `using Greet` can find it. A dependency the lockfile names but the cache lacks is reported, with `tey install` as the fix.

entries.name: dependencyRootsAt
entries.summary: Does what `dependencyRoots` does for the workspace around `start`. A program installed from a path is built in a staged copy, while the working directory may be another project with its own lockfile.

entries.name: sourceDirectoryAt
entries.summary: Returns the directory, relative to the package, that its module names are resolved against. That is `src`, or `.` when package.kex lists top-level source folders with `sources(["app", "config", "db"])`, so that `App.Models.User` is `./app/models/user.kex`. An unreadable manifest gives `src`; callers report the manifest problem themselves.

entries.name: sourceUnit
entries.summary: Returns a file in the source directory as a path relative to the package, the form the compiler is given. A directory of `.` adds nothing in front.

entries.name: sourceUnit?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when a file directly under the source directory is a module to compile. When the package itself is the source directory, its manifests are there too and are skipped.

entries.name: sourceRoots
entries.summary: Returns every `--source-root` a compile of this package needs: its own source directory first, then each dependency's. The order means a module name defined both in the package and in a dependency refers to the package's own module.

entries.name: librarySources
entries.summary: Returns a library's compilable units: every `.kex` file directly under its source directory. Subdirectories are not searched, since a nested module is reached through the file that uses it, and naming it as well would compile it twice and report a duplicate module.

entries.name: librarySourcesAt
entries.summary:
Does what `librarySources` does for the package at `packageRoot`, with the units relative to it. Run the compiler with `packageRoot` as the working directory.

The paths are relative because the compiler registers a module's declarations twice when an entry file is given as an absolute path that is also under a `--source-root`, and then reports a function as "defined twice".

entries.name: backendFlags
entries.summary:
Returns the backend flags for `tey run` and `tey test`: none, so they compile and run on the BEAM like the build that ships, or `-R` for the interpreter when `--interpret` is given.

Processes, `BEAM.*` interop and the String and Char representation differ between the two backends, so a passing interpreter run says little about the built package. `--interpret` is for working around a backend gap or for debugging.

entries.name: runPackage
signatures: runPackage(extra: [String], interpret?: Bool, packageName: String = …) -> Integer

entries.name: runCommand
signatures: runCommand(command: Command, extra: [String], interpret?: Bool) -> Integer
entries.summary:
`tey <name>` for a `command(...)` the manifest declares.

A `.kex` script runs on the selected toolchain with this package's source roots, as `tey run` would, so a release script can `using` the package it releases. Anything else runs as a shell line with `sh -c`, so `command("fmt", run: "kex --format src")` behaves as it would in a terminal, pipes and `&&` included. Extra arguments are passed as `"$@"`, so the shell does not split them again.

entries.name: generate
entries.summary:
`tey generate <namespace>:<generator> [--option value ...] [--force]`

Runs a generator that a direct dependency declares in its `plugin` block. The plugin runs as a child process. It gets the invocation as one line of JSON on stdin and replies with the files it wants written. Tey writes them, only inside the workspace, and asks before replacing a file (`--force` answers yes). The child runs in the operating system's sandbox, with no network and no writing outside scratch space; `--unconfined` lifts that, with a warning.

entries.name: pluginCommand
entries.summary:
`tey plugin <namespace>:<command> [--option value ...]`

Runs a command that a direct dependency declares in its `plugin` block, limited to what the plugin declared and the user approved.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: `tey list`: prints the locked dependencies, then the programs Tey has installed. Outside a project it prints only the programs.

entries.name: buildSelected
signatures: buildSelected(packageName: String, workspace?: Bool, requestedJobs: String = …) -> Integer

entries.name: testReportingFlags
signatures: testReportingFlags(json?: Bool, list?: Bool, only: String) -> [String]
entries.summary:
Returns the compiler flags for how `tey test` reports (kexhq/kex#199).

`--json` prints one JSON record per case, with the file and line of the `it` and of any failure. `--list` prints the cases found without running them, and wins over `--json`. `--only <name>` runs one case or one group.

The flags and the records are the compiler's; Tey only passes them on. Editors run `tey test` because Tey knows the package's source roots (see docs/testing.md).

entries.name: testSpecs
entries.summary: Returns the spec files to run: the ones named on the command line, or every `spec/*.spec.kex` when none are named. Naming one runs a single suite, as an editor's per-file run button does.

entries.name: test
signatures: test(requested: [String], interpret?: Bool, json?: Bool, list?: Bool, only: String) -> Integer

entries.name: testSelected
signatures: testSelected(requested: [String], packageName: String, workspace?: Bool, interpret?: Bool, json?: Bool, list?: Bool, only: String, requestedJobs: String = …) -> Integer
